extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/classics; general readers studying Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Expository/critical analysis of Plato's Republic discussing Plato's objections to poetry and art, the nature of the ideal State, education, and ethical doctrines (e.g., freedom of the will, choice vs. habit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet/painter as imitator (third degree removed from truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: He says that the poet or painter is an imitator, and in the third degree removed from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's image: imitative works are only appearances and not tested by rule and measure. Modern reply noted in text: art is more than imitation—an expression of the ideal in sensible forms. Examples given where artists ennoble base subjects (Rembrandt, Turner) and grand sculpture (Pheidias) may embody something beyond mere imitation; the rule of proportion in great works may be 'higher far than any geometry or arithmetic could express.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor as degradation of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession of an actor was regarded by him as a degradation of human nature, for 'one man in his life' cannot 'play many parts;' the characters which the actor performs seem to destroy his own character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's concern: the actor becomes 'the slave of his art, not the master of it.' He is unable to live his own life while acting many parts. This is advanced as a reason for stronger exclusion of dramatic than epic poets from the Republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative arts express emotion rather than reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato objects to the imitative arts that they express the emotional rather than the rational part of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with Aristotle's catharsis thesis (tragedy purges pity and fear). The text argues that expression of feeling can heal or strengthen emotions and that art can enlist feelings on the side of reason, inspire courage or resignation, suggest infinity, etc. The passage cautions against absolute eradication of emotion and notes art's vocation to present thought as feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets concern the inferior faculties; cannot be rules of life
rubrics_metrics.description: He tells us that ... the poets are concerned with the inferior faculties. The poets are on a level with their own age, but not on a level with Socrates and Plato; and he was well aware that Homer and Hesiod could not be made a rule of life by any process of legitimate interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's view: poets represent particulars and senses rather than universals; they may be suitable to their age but not to philosophical rule. The text also notes Plato's ironic uses of poets and that poets are not reliable interpreters of their own works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets as falsehood-sellers and instruments of tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The poets are also the representatives of falsehood and feigning ... they are the friends of the tyrant, and bask in the sunshine of his patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: despotism uses corrupted literature and false teachers to appeal to the masses; poets at courts (e.g., of Dionysius) prostituted the Muses by praising tyranny. Plato generalizes to false teachers in other ages who serve governments. This is given as a political/moral ground for censoring poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative art's trade-offs: sacrifices between ideal and exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: All imitative art is subject to certain limitations, and therefore necessarily partakes of the nature of a compromise. Something of ideal truth is sacrificed for the sake of the representation, and something in the exactness of the representation is sacrificed to the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite limitations, works of art have a permanent element: they 'idealize and detain the passing thought' and act as intermediates between sense and ideas. The tension between idealization and faithful representation is central to evaluating imitative art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts must be judged by their practical 'good'—not merely 'innocent pleasure'
rubrics_metrics.description: He asks only 'What good have they done?' and is not satisfied with the reply, that 'They have given innocent pleasure to mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's standard evaluates arts by moral/intellectual contribution, not mere entertainment. The text records that in earlier Republic passages Plato admits arts might harmonize as well as enervate, but in Book X he uses a sterner standard (Stoic/Puritan lens) demanding demonstrable good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal poetry as 'hymn of divine perfection' (standards for good poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: There might be a poetry which would be the hymn of divine perfection, the harmony of goodness and truth among men: a strain which should renew the youth of the world ... which might elicit the simple principles, or, as Plato would have called them, the essential forms, of truth and justice out of the variety of opinion and the complexity of modern society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desired features listed: renew world, find materials in present and past, subdue intractable modern materials, elicit essential forms of truth and justice, preserve the good and leave the bad unsung, be based on clear insight into human nature. Examples cited: Aeschylus, Sophocles, Dante, Petrarch, Milton, Wordsworth, Hebrew prophets; Shakespeare ennobles speech and action though 'has left no way of life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's liberty vs. moralizing constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may rebel against any attempt to set limits to his fancy; and he may argue truly that moralizing in verse is not poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tension: while poetry should serve highest truths, poets resist didactic limits. The philosopher's question remains: 'How may the heavenly gift of poesy be devoted to the good of mankind?' — evaluating poetry thus balances artistic freedom against moral aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical variability of poetry's social role
rubrics_metrics.description: In the infancy of mankind, poetry, with the exception of proverbs, is the whole of literature, and the only instrument of intellectual culture; in modern times she is the shadow or echo of her former self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of poetry must consider historical stage: in some ages it is formative and central; in others prose, science, and changing themes (e.g., repeated love-tales) may exhaust its traditional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plato's Spartan-like regulations for the ideal State
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of his regulations are characteristically Spartan; such as the prohibition of gold and silver, the common meals of the men, the military training of the youth, the gymnastic exercises of the women. ... The citizens of Sparta, like Plato’s, were forbidden to trade—they were to be soldiers and not shopkeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of policy-features in the Republic: prohibition of precious metals, communal meals, military emphasis, state-regulated marriage timing and education, prescribed clothing and food, exposure of deformed children, encouragement of male-male friendships to foster bravery, approach to equality of sexes, public marriage, state education for women. These are presented as concrete institutional requirements in Plato's ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradoxes/major structural proposals of the Republic
rubrics_metrics.description: The paradoxes of the Republic, as they have been termed by Morgenstern: (a) the community of property; (b) of families; (c) the rule of philosophers; (d) the analogy of the individual and the State, which, like some other analogies in the Republic, is carried too far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four items are highlighted as distinctive, paradoxical prescriptions of the Republic and form a checklist of its radical structural claims: communal ownership/families, governance by philosophers, and extensive analogies between city and soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education: literary, philosophical, musical, and mathematical training
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato wishes to give his citizens a taste of Athenian freedom as well as of Lacedaemonian discipline. ... There is yet another thread ... the Republic is not only a Dorian State, but a Pythagorean league. ... the great though secondary importance ascribed to mathematics in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational program components: literary and philosophical instruction, cultivation of grace and beauty of life, music (perhaps exaggerated), gymnastic training, Pythagorean-style moral/intellectual regimen, mathematics as important in education, severe training for rulers. These are treated as requirements for preparing citizens and guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: The ideal State is a pattern/vision rather than a practical polity
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing actually existing in the world at all resembles Plato’s ideal State; nor does he himself imagine that such a State is possible. ... he designates the fiction of the earth-born men as 'a noble lie'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Republic's proposals are to be read partly as a theoretical pattern or educational fiction; Plato repeatedly admits unreality of full implementation. This is a criterion for how to interpret and evaluate his laws and proposals: as guiding ideals rather than immediate prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of will and the relation of virtue to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of the will to refuse the evil and to choose the good is distinctly asserted. 'Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her.' ... the virtue which is founded on habit is not sufficient to enable a man to choose; he must add to virtue knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical criterion: moral agency exists within 'walls of necessity' but requires knowledge for correct choice in new situations. Habit alone is an 'inferior sort of goodness'; true practical wisdom requires philosophical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice vs chance: wisdom can overcome adverse lots
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of chance in human life is indicated by the order of the lots. But chance, however adverse, may be overcome by the wisdom of man, if he knows how to choose aright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Odysseus choosing last but wisely. Guidance for moral education: train individuals so that even with unfavorable fortune they can select rightly; again emphasizes need for knowledge over mere routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude in myth/narrative (tale of Er) as credibility device
rubrics_metrics.description: The verisimilitude which is given to the pilgrimage of a thousand years ... add greatly to the probability of the narrative. They are such touches of nature as the art of Defoe might have introduced when he wished to win credibility for marvels and apparitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative credibility criteria: precise incidental details (timings, coincidences, character reactions), plausible small touches, and feigned ignorance about mechanisms (e.g., how Er returned to the body) increase the reader's acceptance of a marvelous tale. Use of Homeric or Oriental elements also affects reception.
